documentation.range: This species was once known from the North and Baltic Seas, English Channel, European coasts of Atlantic, northern Mediterranean west of Rhodos in Greece, and the western and southern Black Sea. It was occasionally recorded in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia. The last record from the Rioni (Georgia) was in 1991, and further surveys have failed to find the species (J. Gessner pers. comm.). Today this species is restricted only to the Garonne River in France.
documentation.population:
Until the beginning of the 20th century, European Sturgeon (A. sturio) was widespread in the tributaries to the Black, Mediterranean and North Seas as well as the eastern Atlantic seaboard. More than 30 major rivers historically had migrating and spawning European Sturgeon. Today only one of these populations is still in existence (the Garonne), although dysfunctional for the past 26 years with the last natural population being confirmed in 1994.
The size of the population today is much smaller (approximately 20–50 wild adult fish). Recovery measures in the Gironde-Garonne-Dordogne Rivers between 1995 and 2015 has resulted in more than 1.6 million juveniles that have been released to support the population (Visser et al. 2020). These have not yet bred in the wild and first breeding (from the releases of 1995) is expected after 2020.
A second small-scale release based upon transfers from France has initiated a population establishment in the Elbe River, Germany, where approximately 20,000 individuals have been released between 2007 and 2015. The survivors of these fish are expected to return to the river after 2020 in small numbers, and further releases will be required to establish a sufficiently large population that can sustain itself.
documentation.habitats:
This is an anadromous species (i.e., it spends at least part of its life in salt water and returns to rivers to breed).

Males reproduce for the first time at 10-12 years, females at 10-20 years. Using the calculation Age of first reproduction + [z * (length of the reproductive period)] (IUCN Standards and Petitions Committee 2019), with z=0.6, average generation length is 66 years; three generations is therefore estimated as approximately 198 years for this species. There are indications for a reproduction at two-year intervals for males and 3–4 years for females in April–July. Adults do not eat during migration and spawning. The distance of the spawning migration seems to be positively correlated with water level, and a distance of 1,000 km or more may be covered during years of high water. Spent fishes immediately return to the sea (FAO 2009).

Potential spawning grounds have been mapped. Juveniles migrate downstream and are present in the upper estuary at one-year-old. They continue a slow downstream migration and penetrate the sea at 2–3 years. For the next 4–6 years, they leave the sea to enter the lower estuary in summer, where movements and feeding were determined. At sea, this species feeds on a variety of molluscs, crustaceans and small fish. The Atlantic population feeds benthically.
documentation.threats: Bycatch is the major threat that has reduced population sizes in the past and currently has the potential to counteract the recovery of self-sustaining populations. The extraction of gravel in the Garonne is a potential threat to the species. Dam construction, pollution and river regulation have led to loss and degradation of spawning and feeding sites. The introduction of alien predators has been identified (OSPAR Commission 2019) to be an important impact upon the recovery of populations.
documentation.measures:
An ongoing in situ conservation programme is in place. Ex situ conservation is carried out in France and Germany. A species-specific Bern Convention Action Plan has been developed, with National Action Plans being in place or under development in France, Germany and the Netherlands.

Restocking was initiated after the first successful controlled reproductions in 1995 and commenced in 2007 until 2014. Survival rate for the 1995 stocking is 3-5%; the survival rate of recent releases is dependent upon the age and size at release. For the first time in 2007, progenies were obtained from individuals maintained in an ex situ stock (Williot et al. 2009).

There are coordinated fisheries awareness programs in place in the Eastern Atlantic North and North Sea range countries.

This species was listed on CITES Appendix II in 1975, and moved to Appendix I in 1983.
documentation.use_trade:
In the past (until the late 19th century), juveniles of this species were harvested as animal food in Poland and Germany (J. Gessner pers. comm.).

100% removal from the wild - This relates to the past only as commercial trade in this species is now prohibited.
documentation.rationale:
European Sturgeon (Acipenser sturio) has undergone a reduction in population size by more than 99% over the three generation period (approximately 198 years). The subpopulation in the Gironde (France) is actively supported and the numbers of fish observed in the estuary and the coastal waters are increasing. The first fish of reproductive age were observed to return to the river in 2020 (Rochard pers. comm.).

Despite these positive signals, the species is massively under pressure with a reduced area of occupancy (AOO), which has declined by more than 95%. The adult population comprises no more than 50 individuals, and reproduction in the wild has been suspended since 1994.

Based upon the past population decline and the extremely small number of mature fish in the wild, as well as the persisting threats from habitat loss and bycatch, the species is assessed as Critically Endangered (CR).
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Archaelogical remains suggest that Acipenser sturio colonised the Baltic Sea about 3,000 years ago from the North Sea, and vanished from the Baltic Sea about 800 years ago. Climatic changes about 100 years ago (Little Ice Age) might have had an impact indirectly in favouring introgression by hybridization with A. oxyrinchus.
